questions.short_title: Big community arrest programme didn't change survival
questions.question: A large cluster-randomised trial tested a community and EMS programme bundling telecommunicator CPR training, community CPR training and better AED use. What did it find for survival with good neurological outcome?
options: A benefit only in younger patients
A reduction in survival compared with usual care
About a 9% absolute improvement over usual care
No meaningful difference from usual care
questions.explanation: Survival with good neurological outcome was essentially the same: 9.0% with the intervention versus 9.4% with usual care. Because the programme bundled four components together, the trial can't tell whether one element, like telecommunicator CPR instructions, drove the null result.

questions.short_title: Risk scores sort survival odds in paediatric OHCA
questions.question: The paediatric OHCA risk scores grouped children into low, moderate and high survival categories using which of the following?
options: Only age, with outcomes otherwise identical across the groups
Hospital interventions including length of resuscitation and drug doses given
Post-arrest EEG results and imaging findings from the receiving hospital
Prehospital variables such as bystander CPR, first rhythm and arrest location
questions.explanation: The scores were built entirely from variables known before hospital arrival, like gender, witness status, aetiology, bystander CPR, prehospital AED use and first rhythm. They were only internally validated, so they're hypothesis-generating rather than bedside-ready.

questions.short_title: How common are blood-borne infections in first responders
questions.question: Which blood-borne infection had the highest pooled prevalence among prehospital first responders in this review?
options: MRSA colonisation
Hepatitis C
HIV
Hepatitis B
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B pooled at 6.2%, above MRSA at about 4% and hepatitis C at 1.8%. The estimates came from very heterogeneous studies that mixed paramedics with police and firefighters, so treat them as rough.

questions.short_title: GCS-based triage misses seriously injured trauma patients
questions.question: In this cohort of patients flagged by EMS as suspected severe trauma, what did a GCS of 9–15 suggest about underlying injury severity?
options: Roughly half met the anatomical criterion
Only rural patients in this group were severely injured
One in ten of these patients met the anatomical severity criterion
These patients never had severe injuries on hospital diagnosis
questions.explanation: 10.0% of patients with GCS 9–15 met the diagnosis-based anatomical severity criterion, so a normal-ish GCS doesn't rule out serious injury. The severity measure was post-hoc and diagnosis-based, and undertriage definitions vary between systems, so treat this as hypothesis-generating.

questions.short_title: Rhythm changes during CPR track neurological outcomes
questions.question: In the registry study of nonshockable OHCA, how did rhythm changes during CPR relate to good neurological outcome at discharge?
options: Asystole converting to PEA did better than persistent asystole, and persistent PEA did best
PEA deteriorating to asystole had worse outcomes than patients who never had PEA at all
Any rhythm transition, in either direction, carried the same prognosis as persistent asystole
Only patients whose rhythm stayed the same throughout CPR had good outcomes
questions.explanation: Asystole-to-PEA roughly doubled the odds of good outcome versus persistent asystole, and persistent PEA did best (OR 8.70). Keep in mind the absolute differences were tiny (0.1 to 0.9 percentage points), and rhythm transitions may just track how the arrest is going rather than change it.

questions.short_title: Sepsis suspicion at dispatch, earlier antibiotics
questions.question: When dispatch flagged suspected sepsis, what was the adjusted difference in time from ED arrival to antibiotics?
options: About 31 minutes shorter
About 60 minutes shorter
About 31 minutes longer
No meaningful difference
questions.explanation: Sepsis suspicion at dispatch was associated with a 31-minute shorter adjusted time to antibiotics and higher odds of antibiotics within 60 minutes. Only 31 of 115 triaged patients carried the flag, so the finding is hypothesis-generating.

questions.short_title: 3% of callers drive a fifth of all calls
questions.question: How did post-threshold calls from frequent callers differ from calls before they reached the frequent-caller threshold?
options: More often conveyed to hospital after dispatch
More often categorised as unclear problem at dispatch
More often given high-priority ambulance dispatch
More often resolved by phone and ended without transport
questions.explanation: Calls after the fifth-call threshold were more often resolved over the phone (23.8%) and ended in non-conveyance (27.4%) than pre-threshold calls. The finding comes from a single Danish region with a dispatch-based definition of frequent calling, so it may not map directly onto Australian systems.

questions.short_title: US naloxone use varies by region, not rurality
questions.question: After adjusting for clinical factors, what did this US study find about rural versus urban naloxone administration during suspected opioid overdose?
options: Rural odds were nearly double urban odds
Rural odds were essentially the same as urban odds
Rural odds were clearly lower than urban odds
Rural odds were higher only for fentanyl-involved cases
questions.explanation: The rural-versus-urban association attenuated to null (aOR 1.01) once clinical factors like fentanyl involvement, cardiac arrest and acuity were adjusted for. The raw rural-urban gap appears to have reflected case-mix rather than genuine treatment differences, and the authors note documented naloxone use is a surveillance marker, not a clinical endpoint.
